title: Autonomy, Explanation and Evidence in Belief Revision
abstract: Across three studies (n = 155) adolescent learners freely investigated a multivariable database to ascertain the extent to which their initial beliefs were affirmed or warranted revision. Our purpose was (a) to examine the strategies used (Studies 1-3), (b) to identify the respective roles of explanation and evidence in the process (Studies 1-3), and (c) investigate the role of autonomy (Studies 2 and 3). Participants were randomly assigned to one of three conditions. In Condition 1, explanations were solicited prior to and following data investigation. In Condition 2, explanations were solicited only following data investigation, and in Condition 3, no explanations were solicited. Participants completed an autonomy assessment pre- and post-random assignment to three conditions manipulating explanations. Consistent were the ways in which explanation influenced beliefs and benefitted belief revision. title: The Principle of Receivable-Based National Development: A Doctrinal Shift from Debt-Financed State Development
abstract: This article proposes a transformative doctrinal shift in state development financing, moving from debt-financed growth toward receivable-based national development . Post-war development orthodoxy has institutionalized sovereign borrowing as a primary financing tool, inadvertently embedding states in a cycle of long-term liabilities, fiscal dependency, and recurrent crises. Drawing on the intersections of law and political economy, this article argues that debt-based development is not merely a technical policy choice but a restrictive doctrinal framework that erodes sovereignty and constrains democratic fiscal autonomy. As a normative alternative, it conceptualizes the state as a sovereign creditor —endowed with enforceable legal and economic claims, including taxation authority, natural resource entitlements, state-owned enterprise revenues, and international receivables. These assets can be mobilized to finance development without accumulating new debt. title: Data literacy across disciplines: Context, language, and technology in K-12 learning
abstract: Integrating data literacy into K-12 education in an increasingly data-driven society is imperative. Data literacy is conceptualized as an interdisciplinary competence that extends beyond traditional statistical understanding, encompassing skills in accessing, analyzing, interpreting, and communicating insights from data. Drawing on sociocultural theory, this paper argues that the formalisms-first pedagogical approach is theoretically limited, rooted in a conception of learning that strips away the social, cultural, and material conditions through which meaningful data reasoning develops. In contrast, we advocate for inquiry-driven strategies like project-based and problem-based learning, which restore the contextual, collaborative conditions that make data literacy learnable. Central to this argument is the claim that data literacy is best understood as a disciplinary language, a set of representational, argumentative, and interpretive practices acquired through socially scaffolded participation. title: Acceptance and Colour Preference of Nursing Uniform in Bangladesh: A Descriptive Comparative Study
abstract: Background It is well known that uniforms convey identity, discipline, and professionalism in nursing. In many countries, nursing uniforms are regulated institutionally. Bangladesh, however, has a national policy that regulate colour and style of nursing uniform. Concerns have emerged regarding the acceptance of current olive-coloured uniform among nursing community. This study aimed to explore acceptance of the current uniform and colour preferences in Bangladesh. Methods This cross-sectional study was conducted among nurses and nursing students in Bangladesh from May 18, 2025, to August 2, 2025. Participants were recruited through convenience sampling. Acceptance of the current olive-coloured uniform was assessed using an eight-item measure. Descriptive statistics summarized participant characteristics and colour preferences. Mann–Whitney U and Kruskal–Wallis tests were used to explore differences across groups. Data were analyzed using R version 4.5.2. title: Between Custom and Constitution: Intersectional Bias Against Women in Plural Legal Systems in Nigeria and South Africa
abstract: In most post-colonial African states, customary law coexists with constitutional frameworks. This coexistence often creates extra disadvantages for women whose intersecting identities such as gender, socioeconomic status, and sometimes religion heighten their vulnerabilities. This paper examines institutional bias in Nigeria and South Africa’s plural legal orders. It focuses on how tensions between patriarchal customary norms and equality-oriented constitutional provisions create unique disadvantages for women in family law domains such as marriage, divorce, and property rights. In Nigeria, despite landmark rulings like the Supreme Court decision in Ukeje v Ukeje invalidating male primogeniture under Igbo custom as unconstitutional, enforcement gaps persist due to weak integration of customary and statutory systems. These gaps leave women especially rural, low-income women from ethnic minorities vulnerable to exclusion. In South Africa, progressive jurisprudence has played a significant role in advancing living customary law. title: Constrained triadic reciprocal determinism: advancing social cognitive theory through an exploration of informal learning in paediatric communication among medical students
abstract: Purpose This study explores the role of informal learning in the development of competent communication skills among medical students interacting with paediatric patients. By investigating the interplay between personal, environmental, and behavioural factors, the study aims to identify how clinical placements facilitate or hinder communication proficiency. Ultimately, the research seeks to advance Bandura’s Social Cognitive Theory by contextualising its constructs within the high-stakes, opportunistic learning environment of undergraduate medical education. Methods Adopting a relativist ontology and an interpretivist epistemology, the study utilised a qualitative phenomenological methodology. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with eight senior medical students (Years 4 and 5) from the University of Leicester. Data were analysed using Braun and Clarke’s reflexive thematic analysis. This approach allowed for a deep exploration of the lived experience of informal learning, ensuring that the findings were grounded in the subjective realities of the participants. title: Power Dynamics: Technological Fragmentation in U.S.-China Rivalry
abstract: The intensifying technological rivalry between the U.S. and China has become one of the central arenas through which contemporary power politics is being reorganized. In the existing literature, this rivalry is often viewed either as a broad contest for technological supremacy or as an early stage of full decoupling. However, this paper advances a more specific claim: the rivalry is producing selective, security-driven fragmentation of technological ecosystems rather than either imminent war or complete technological separation. The argument is developed through a qualitative structured comparison of three issue areas: advanced semiconductors, artificial intelligence, and technical standardization. The selected cases link technological capability to national security, market power, institutional rule-making, and the distribution of international influence. The paper examines Power Transition Theory (PTT) by showing that sector-specific technological leadership cannot be mechanically translated into aggregate national power parity. title: Feedback engagement strategies and metrics for customers in vulnerable circumstances: An empty rapid review and recommendations for further research
abstract: Across sectors, there is an increasing recognition of the need to identify and support consumers in vulnerable situations. To assess whether existing support measures are effective and how they might be improved, satisfaction surveys are commonly used. However, low response rates and the under-representation of the most vulnerable groups limit their usefulness. Moreover, it remains unclear whether these surveys effectively measure what they intend to. A rapid review of the evidence was conducted to (i) identify barriers and explore strategies to increase participation in feedback mechanisms among consumers experiencing vulnerability, and (ii) examine the availability and use of (validated) feedback or satisfaction measures for these groups. The review protocol was pre-registered on the Open Science Framework (https://osf.io/tqnvr). Searches were conducted in Web of Science and ProQuest Social Science databases in July 2025. No eligible reports met the inclusion criteria. This absence of evidence highlights a substantial gap in understanding how to design inclusive and reliable feedback processes for consumers in vulnerable circumstances. title: Digital Payment Adoption and Cross-Border Trade Efficiency Among Small and Medium Enterprises in East Africa
abstract: Background Small and medium enterprises (SMEs) dominate East African commerce yet incur persistent time, cost, and liquidity frictions when settling cross-border transactions. Digital payment technologies promise to ease these constraints, but rigorous evidence connecting adoption to measurable trade-process efficiency is sparse. Purpose This study evaluates whether, and under what institutional conditions, SME digital-payment adoption improves cross-border trade efficiency in Kenya, Uganda, Rwanda, and Tanzania. Methods A harmonised dataset pools 2023–2025 World Bank Enterprise Surveys microdata with country-level indicators of payment-system interoperability and Trade Facilitation Agreement (TFA) progress. Adoption is captured through the shares of sales and purchases conducted electronically, while efficiency is proxied by customs-clearance days, compliance costs, and perceived predictability. Ordinary least squares models with survey-design inference estimate adoption–efficiency associations; interaction terms test moderation by interoperability and regulatory alignment. title: Socio-cultural determinants delaying Black men's health-seeking behaviour in the public primary health care settings of Ga-Rankuwa, Pretoria, South Africa
abstract: The rapid process of social change which took place in South African society from the beginning of the last century has had many negative effects on the lives of the majority of the country’s Black population. Black men in particular have been the most affected group. Reportedly, this is the group that has been more at risk of premature morbidity and death due to preventable diseases of various kinds. Yet, a significant number of studies have shown that Black men are the least consumers of the public primary health care facilities and services available to them. The main aim of this article was to explore how social and cultural determinants of health-seeking behaviour (HSB) shaped their response to ill-health. A contextual, descriptive and explorative research design was used, based on 15 purposively sampled research participants (Black men) between the ages of 25 and 66 years, who lived in the township of Ga-Rankuwa, Pretoria, City of Tshwane Metropolitan Municipality (Gauteng Province, South Africa). The primary data for the study were collected by using in-depth semi-structured interviews, and were thematically analysed by using the “seven steps approach to thematic analysis”.

title: Global Standards for Athlete-Centred Governance: 20% Peer-Elected Representation
abstract: Despite a growing global shift toward athlete-centred approaches in sport governance, a significant decision-making gap persists where athletes are often relegated to advisory roles without formal voting authority. This consultative approach to athlete representation leaves sport organizations vulnerable to risk, particularly regarding athlete protection, well-being, and accountability.. This policy brief suggests that, for athlete-centered sport governance to be meaningful, two global criteria should be applied: (1) a minimum of 20% athlete voting representation; and (2) peer-elected positions. Grounded in critical mass theory, a threshold of 15–30% representation by a minority group is generally required for a meaningful shift in a board or committee culture. Based on legislative examples and recommendations from athlete advocacy organizations (e.g., the Ted Stevens Olympic and Amateur Sports Act and AthletesCAN), a 20% minimum criterion is both legitimate and supported by converging theoretical and policy evidence as a minimum baseline. In addition, legitimacy can be enhanced by the peer election of athletes, rather than through appointment by sport organizational administrators

title: Structured Review Panels and Perceived Procedural Justice on Performance Appraisal Systems: Implications for Academic Staff Retention in Higher Education Institutions.
abstract: Performance appraisal systems in higher education institutions play a critical role in shaping academic staff development, motivation, accountability and retention. However, concerns about fairness and transparency in appraisal processes continue to undermine their effectiveness. This study examines the role of structured review panels in shaping perceived procedural justice on performance appraisal systems and explores its implications for academic staff retention in higher education institutions. Grounded on Organisational Justice Theory, the paper conceptualises structured review panels as institutional mechanisms that enhance consistency, transparency, and accountability in appraisal decisions. Through a conceptual synthesis of literature, the study argues that structured review panels strengthen perceived procedural fairness by reducing bias, improving decision legitimacy, and enhancing trust in institutional processes. In turn, higher levels of perceived procedural justice are associated with increased job satisfaction, organisational commitment, and reduced turnover intentions among academic staff. title: Intentional Mentorship Programs and Information Transparency as Drivers of Perceived Organisational Justice in Higher Education Institutions
abstract: Higher education institutions increasingly rely on talent management systems to strengthen academic performance and staff development. However, perceptions of organisational justice remain uneven, often undermining the effectiveness of mentorship and communication systems. This study examines how intentional mentorship programs and information transparency influence perceived organisational justice in higher education institutions. Grounded in Organisational Justice Theory, the paper conceptualises mentorship intentionality and transparency as key relational and structural mechanisms that shape fairness perceptions among academic staff. Using a conceptual and narrative synthesis of existing literature, the study argues that structured and purpose-driven mentorship programs enhance interactional and procedural justice by improving guidance, support, and career development clarity. Similarly, transparent information systems strengthen distributive and procedural justice by ensuring equitable access to opportunities and decision-making processes. title: What is Extinction? Ecopolitics of the End
abstract: In recent years, extinction has become something of a buzzword used to portray the state of consciousness of the epoch. Its definition as a concept, however, heavily oscillates between naturalistic, speculative, ethical and critical connotations. The aim of this paper is to build an original position around some of the most relevant issues raised by the concept of extinction, such as the position of humankind as both its perpetrator and victim, the role of extinction management in contemporary biocapitalism and a possible critical engagement with catastrophe that avoids both paralysis and underestimation. The first section addresses some aspects of the question on ‘what is extinction’ starting from its biological meaning and elaborating on its ontological implications. The second section scrutinizes two relevant approaches to extinction within contemporary humanities, that is speculative realism and extinction studies, and highlights their respective shortcomings. title: Extralegal Factors in Evaluating Muslim Defendants: Impact of Juror’s Identity and Stereotypic Crime on Sentencing, Fairness, and Leniency
abstract: What impact does a mock juror’s identity salience have on the evaluation of a Muslim defendant based on the type of crime that was allegedly committed? In study 1, mock jurors, who were college students, had their religious/moral/spiritual/control identity primed and evaluated the case of a Muslim (or religion unstated) defendant who was allegedly the accomplice to a crime stereotyped to be religiously motivated (terrorism) or not (arson). Mock jurors were harsher when judging terrorism (rather than arson) and a defendant with an unstated religion (rather than being Muslim, contrary to hypotheses). Study 2 sought to generalize these results to a more representative sample to reflect the composition of a real jury by using MTurk workers, while testing if there was a leniency bias toward the Muslim defendants. Study 2 found that when a moral identity was salient, more leniency was given to the Muslim defendant, regardless of the type of crime allegedly committed. This has implications for identifying factors to train jurors and lawyers to foster greater impartiality for defendants.

title: Challenges, Support, and Progression for Autistic Students in University: A Systematic Review
abstract: Background An increasing number of autistic students are entering Higher Education (HE), yet they continue to face significant challenges, including elevated rates of mental health difficulties and limited access to appropriate support. These students are also less likely to achieve academic success or graduate compared to their neurotypical peers. Despite growing awareness, there is limited synthesis of university-based initiatives aimed at supporting the mental health and wellbeing (MHWB) of autistic students. This systematic review explores barriers to engagement and identifies effective MHWB support practices within HE settings. Methods A systematic search of seven academic databases was conducted to identify studies published between 2015 and 2025 that focused on MHWB support for autistic university students. Following a multi-stage screening process, eligible studies were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. Results Nineteen studies met the inclusion criteria. title: Improving implementation of Making Every Contact Count: Lessons learned from research across multiple projects from 2017-2025
abstract: Making Every Contact Count (MECC) is a person-centred, opportunistic approach embedding health behaviour change conversations across services, central to UK prevention strategy. Despite its potential to promote healthier lifestyles and address health inequalities, translating MECC principles into routine practice remains complex. This synthesis consolidates findings from collaborative research (2017–2025) exploring implementation barriers and enablers across diverse English settings. This synthesis integrates findings from 12 studies (2017–2025) examining Making Every Contact Count (MECC) across the North East and North Cumbria, regional NHS Foundation Trusts, and national partners. Using qualitative, quantitative, and mixed methods approaches—including strategic behavioural analyses, fidelity assessments, and routine data—the studies explored MECC design, delivery, training models (including Train-the-Trainer), and implementation contexts. Data sources encompassed interviews with trainers, trainees, and service users, alongside document analysis and quantitative metrics of knowledge, confidence, and fidelity. title: The dynamic interplay of ‘political space’ and language activism in education LP development in Pakistan: A historical analysis and lessons learnt
abstract: Pakistan’s language policy (LP) has historically reinforced hierarchies privileging Urdu and English over indigenous languages, contributing to persistent patterns of linguistic and educational exclusion. Drawing on the findings of a politico-historical review of 91 scholarly and grey literature sources, this policy brief examines how shifts in political structures have shaped LP development and language activism (LA) in education. It situates these dynamics within wider struggles for equity, recognising LP as both a policy product and a site of contestation where actors negotiate linguistic power and educational access. Findings reveal that LP evolution in Pakistan has been non-linear, shaped by cycles of contestation and negotiation between state control and activism. Three key phases are identified: (1) Centralised and Exclusionary LP (1947–1971)—marked by nation-building and Urdu dominance; (2) Gradual Recognition of Linguistic Rights (1972–2009): featuring partial accommodation of regional languages; and (3) Decentralised and Participatory LP (2010–present), seemingly enabled by the 18th Amendment’s devolution of education. title: Barriers to evidence-based practice by course leaders in a small-specialist land-based higher education institution: a grounded theory study
abstract: Background This study focuses on course leadership in small specialist higher education institutions. Course leaders are pivotal members of the academic team whose role bridges the interests of all institutional stakeholders. In small-specialist Higher Education Institutions, course-leader roles typically include the pastoral care of students, curriculum development, quality assurance, admissions, course marketing, and mentoring of colleagues. Despite the importance of this role, course leadership has been under-researched. The limited research available focuses on the role itself, rather than course leader practice, with little recognition of how course leaders use EBP. Therefore, the purpose of this research is to explain how course leaders use evidence to inform their practice in small specialist HEIs. Methods This study uses a grounded theory approach to investigate evidence-based course leadership. Semi-structured interviews were held, after which transcripts were coded and analyzed through constant comparison and intensive memoing. title: How to Write with Trees: Material Ecocritical Strategies for Multispecies Care in Contemporary Fiction
abstract: This study explores how contemporary literature writes with trees, rather than merely about them, attending to the entangled lives of humans and nonhumans. Drawing on material ecocriticism perspectives, it examines how storytelling can foster care, attention, and ethical imagination in multispecies worlds. The analysis focuses on three novels: Elif Shafak’s The Island of Missing Trees , Ursula K. Le Guin’s The Word for World Is Forest , and Barbara Kingsolver’s Prodigal Summer. Each text employs different writing strategies against anthropocentrism. title: Power Dynamics: The Technological Rivalry between the U.S. and China
abstract: The intensifying technological competition between the United States and China is redefining the global power dynamics in the realm of international politics. This competition spans critical domains, including artificial intelligence, semiconductor manufacturing, quantum computing, nanotechnology, and biomedical engineering. Both nations seek to secure a first-mover advantage in these strategic sectors driven by geopolitical and economic motives. The COVID-19 pandemic has accelerated global digital transformation, further amplifying the significance of technological supremacy in shaping geopolitics (O'Toole et al., 2020). The Russia-Ukraine conflict underscored the transformative impact of advanced technologies such as unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) and artificial intelligence on modern warfare, raising pertinent questions regarding the trajectory of technological innovation and its implications for global patterns. To explore this complex landscape, this study aims to address several key research questions. First, it examines the nature and scope of the current technological rivalry between the US and China. title: Rhythmic Structure, Working Memory Capacity, and Chunking in the Perception of Unfamiliar Long Rhythmic Cycles
abstract: Research on rhythm perception has largely focused on short rhythmic structures typical in Western music, leaving a gap in the understanding of the perception of longer and complex rhythmic cycles found in other musical traditions. North Indian Classical Music (NICM) features long rhythmic cycles varying in structure, duration, and number of beats. These rhythmic cycles exist in the NICM tradition and go beyond the known limits of working memory and psychological present (2–3 seconds). This study investigates how unfamiliar musicians, with no prior exposure to NICM, perceive these long rhythmic cycles, focusing on working memory capacity and chunking strategy. Participants completed a rhythm discrimination task involving NICM cycles that varied in duration, number of beats, and rhythmic structure (isochronous vs. non-isochronous). The study also contained a digit-span task to assess memory capacity, followed by selecting a visualised grouping structure of the rhythmic cycle. title: Exploring the utilization of the legal system during COVID-19 among Black women intimate partner violence survivors
abstract: Background During the COVID-19 pandemic, the legal system was temporarily restructured to adhere to the recommended disease mitigation strategies. However, the pandemic also exacerbated the prevalence and intensity of intimate partner violence, especially among Black women. This led to Black women IPV survivors having to engage with the restructured legal system as a method of formal support to navigate their relationships. Through an intersectional lens, this study explores how Black women IPV survivors navigated the legal system amid the service disruptions of the global pandemic. Methods In the first half of 2021, 50 Black women IPV survivors who were engaged with domestic violence organizations were purposively recruited to participate in a one-time, semi-structured qualitative interview. Findings were analyzed using a combined thematic and interpretative phenomenological analysis. Findings Two themes emerged as Black women IPV survivors discussed their experiences with the legal system during the COVID-19 pandemic: (1) failed protection from lack of granted protective orders and (2) ineffective legal proceedings. title: Remembering Witches: Missing Memorials and the Reimagining of the Historic Sorcery Trials in Agder
abstract: In the 2010s, public memorials commemorating historical witch trials have appeared in several countries, including Norway. However, in the southern region of Agder, no official recognition of the historic witch trials exist. This article describes the 2024 interdisciplinary project Remembering Witches, which asked what it means to forget and remember the trials in the region and beyond. First, we examine how alternative forms of memory culture—including research, artworks, literature, and public discourse—have addressed this absence by reinterpreting the figure of the witch in Agder. Second, we document our efforts to foster public dialogue about a potential local memorial, involving university students, artists, scholars, and musicians. Throughout we draw on scholarship about dark tourism and memorialisation, including Ann Rigney’s concept of ‘disabled memories’ to consider how the memory of the so-called witches of Agder became inactive, and how it might resurface again. title: Lalla Ded the Philosopher-Saint: Exploring Hagiography, Mysticism and Intellectual Discourses in Kashmiri Vaakhs
abstract: This paper offers a critical evaluation of Lalla Ded, the fourteenth-century mystic, as a philosopher-saint. Her vaakhs form a body of intellectual and spiritual discourses. Rather than looking at her vaakhs solely through the biographical lens, the paper approaches the vaakhs as a site for philosophical inquiry on the nature of self, divinity, mysticism and social order. The interdisciplinary nature encompassing philosophy, theology and social critique calls for an analytical framework that captures the conversational depth of the vaakhs . The paper interrogates the core tensions in the vaakhs using critical discourse analysis as an analytical framework. The vaakhs reflect her role as a spiritual force, transcending religious divisions and holding significance in contemporary intellectual debates. While scholars describe the vaakh as a verse, saying, song, and proverb, this paper argues for understanding vaakh as ‘poetic discourse’, foregrounding its philosophical dimension. title: Governance Networks in Crisis: Time to Recognise the Problems?
abstract: Managing through policy networks has been a perennial element of the governing task. Modern analysts of government, public policy and public administration evolved theories of policy networks and public management. Key to the development of network analysis and theories of governance was the concept of complex interdependence. Conceptual models came to mirror the complexities of the network theory they sought to explain, while stress and crisis increasingly exposed flaws in both theory and practice, revealing a series of overlapping problems: accountability lacunae, performance failures, ideological capture, and standards and ethics challenges. These produced increased public frustration, and contributed to rising populist demands for less complex and more transparent government, with ‘stronger’ central leadership. However, the inherent complexities of government, and the inevitability of working through policy networks mean that there are no simple solutions to these problems. title: Nature, Narrative and Eco-Orientalism in The White Tiger (2008): A Post-Colonial study
abstract: This article explores the environmental narratives in Abiga’s book The White Tiger (2008) through the lens of Eco-Orientalism. This study explores Adiga’s depiction of ecological degradation and post-colonial identity in contemporary India on Western casts conceptions. It examines how The White Tiger (2008) highlights and challenges the eco-orientalist discourse. It illustrates the struggles of Balram Halwai, the main character of the novel, travels across a panorama of rural and urban exploited life, represented dirty air, and disregarded places like Delhi. These environmental concerns identify persons impacted by poverty, social inequality, and challenging society as being ecologically primitive. This research gives a new perspective on environmental discourse in Indian literature and reevaluates nature storytelling in emerging-economy contexts by using ecological Orientalism theory to this Indian fiction. This research uses qualitative method to explore fast industrialization and contaminated urban surroundings. This novel challenges reader to engage critically with socioeconomic interconnections in the globe through oversimplified success conception of Balram’s story. Essential

title: What does transformation in Higher Education research culture look like? Evidence from action research within a diverse post-1992 department
abstract: Transforming research culture and environment has been a priority for UK Research and Innovation (UKRI) and has been reflected in recent rounds of the UK Research Excellence Framework (REF). Broadly, research culture encompasses the behaviours, values, expectations, attitudes and norms of research communities and is advanced via areas of academic service in mentoring, skills development, leadership, standards and local development opportunities. There is need to understand how academic units can develop research activity in such a way as to meet criteria of excellence and intensivity within a highly pressured UK Higher Education sector. In this article, we set out the process and outcome of a programme of research culture transformation within an archetypal post-1992 department at Northumbria University in the Northeast of England. Framed around the prospective content of REF People, Culture and Environment (PCE) and Impact narratives, we argue that there are clear means of meeting criteria that protect colleagues by increasing external sources of funding. title: Remembering Witches: Missing memorials and the Historic Sorcery Trials in Southern Norway
abstract: In the 2010s, public memorials commemorating historical witch trials have appeared in several countries, including Norway. However, in the southern region of Agder, no official recognition of the historic witch trials exist. This article describes the 2024 interdisciplinary project Remembering Witches, which asked what it means to forget and remember the trials in the region and beyond. First, we examine how alternative forms of memory culture—including research, artworks, literature, and public discourse—have addressed this absence by reinterpreting the figure of the witch in Agder. Second, we document our efforts to foster public dialogue about a potential local memorial, involving university students, artists, scholars, and musicians. Throughout we draw on Ann Rigney’s concept of ‘disabled memories’ to consider how the memory of the so-called witches of Agder became inactive, and how it might resurface again. We also compare the lack of engagement with this history in Southern Norway to the activity in Northern Norway, where an ambitious, large and impactful memorial to local trials serves as a counterexample, or perhaps guiding star. title: Institutionalising One Health Strategies for Addressing Antimicrobial Resistance in the Environment in the Context of Scottish-UK Governance Dynamics
abstract: Background Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) presents a complex global health challenge requiring coordinated responses across human, animal, and environmental sectors. This study explores how a One Health approach to AMR is being implemented within the United Kingdom’s and Scotland’s multi-level governance frameworks, with a particular focus on the integration of environmental considerations. Methods The research draws on qualitative data from semi-structured interviews with stakeholders across government, academia, and relevant sectors. The analysis examines multisectoral collaboration, governance structures, leadership, and mechanisms for accountability and evaluation, using the 2019–2024 UK National Action Plan for AMR as a contextual frame. Results Findings highlight the importance of strategic coherence and goal alignment in navigating complex governance arrangements. Effective implementation of One Health principles depends on coordination across health, environmental, and academic sectors. title: How to Write with Trees: Ecofeminist Strategies for Multispecies Care in Contemporary Fiction
abstract: This study explores how contemporary literature writes with trees, rather than merely about them, attending to the entangled lives of humans and nonhumans. Drawing on ecofeminist perspectives, it examines how storytelling can foster care, attention, and ethical imagination in multispecies worlds. The analysis focuses on three novels: Elif Şafak’s The Island of Missing Trees , Ursula K. Le Guin’s The Word for World Is Forest , and Barbara Kingsolver’s Prodigal Summer . Each text employs different writing strategies against anthropocentrism. In Şafak, a fig tree witnesses and remembers alongside human characters; in Le Guin, the Athshe forest enacts a collective consciousness that resists human mastery; and in Kingsolver, chestnut trees participate in relational ecologies that intertwine with Appalachian human and nonhuman lives. Across these narratives, trees are not passive symbols but active, communicating participants that co-create the worlds they inhabit. The authors employ three key strategies for multispecies care. title: The Mental Health Consequences of Non-Disclosure Agreements on Survivors of Workplace Discriminatory Harassment and Abuse
abstract: This paper examines how non-disclosure agreements (NDAs), when used to resolve allegations of workplace discriminatory harassment and abuse, function not as neutral legal resolutions but as mechanisms of secondary traumatization. By legally mandating silence, NDAs compound the powerlessness survivors experienced during the original assault into a binding contract, creating a persistent psychological injury that endures long after the precipitating events have ended. First, NDAs obstruct evidence-based trauma treatments, such as Prolonged Exposure, Cognitive Processing Therapy, and EMDR, that require survivors to recount and process their traumatic memories, thereby rendering these modalities clinically infeasible. Second, enforced secrecy severs survivors from essential support networks, preventing disclosure to family, friends, and partners, and fostering shame, isolation, and mistrust—each of which undermines relational healing and is known to predict poorer recovery outcomes. title: Influence of Memory and Chunking Strategies in the Perception of Culturally Unfamiliar Long Rhythmic Cycles.
abstract: Research on rhythm perception has largely focused on short rhythmic cycles typical in Western music, leaving a gap in the understanding of the perception of longer and complex rhythmic structures found in other musical traditions. North Indian Classical Music (NICM) features long rhythmic cycles varying in structure, duration, and number of beats. These rhythms exist in the NICM tradition and go beyond the known limits of working memory and psychological present (2–3 seconds). This study investigates how unfamiliar musicians, with no prior exposure to NICM, perceive these long rhythmic cycles, focusing on working memory capacity and chunking strategy. Participants completed a rhythm discrimination task involving NICM cycles that varied in duration, number of beats, and rhythmic structure (isochronous vs. non-isochronous). The study also contained a digit-span task to assess memory capacity, followed by selecting a grouping structure visualising the pattern.
